# The Review Process {#sec-review-process} Peer review is the institution through which a scholarly field decides what counts as knowledge. A manuscript becomes a published contribution only after anonymous experts have judged it interesting, valid, and important enough to add to the record, and the editor has aggregated those judgments into a decision. For the author the process is a gauntlet; for the field it is a screening technology that trades speed for reliability. This chapter treats reviewing from both sides of the desk. It traces how peer review arose, what journals are for, and how the publishing system is organized; it then explains what an editor and a set of reviewers actually do to a submission, how a competent review is structured, and—because reviewing is at bottom a measurement problem—how to think formally about the reliability of the verdicts that emerge. The chapter is also practical. A marketing PhD will referee dozens of papers before ever publishing many, and learning to review well is the fastest route to understanding what separates a strong paper from a rejected one. We therefore move from the **motivation** for reviewing, to the **mechanics** of the editorial pipeline, to the **anatomy** of a good referee report, to a **statistical** account of reviewer agreement and the noise inherent in the system. Throughout, the standard exemplar is the *Journal of Marketing* (JM), whose published review policy is unusually explicit; the principles transfer to the rest of the top-tier marketing journals (@sec-introduction).[^jm-policy] [^jm-policy]: The *Journal of Marketing* documents its review philosophy and its data-transparency requirements in publicly posted editorial statements. The norms described here—turnaround targets, the criteria reviewers weigh, the structure of a report—are paraphrased from those statements and from the broader editorial practice of the marketing top-4 (JM, JMR, *Marketing Science*, *Journal of Consumer Research*). ## A Short History of Peer Review {#sec-review-history} External peer review is younger than the scientific journal, and much younger than most researchers assume. For most of the history of scientific publishing, the decision to print rested with an editor or a society committee, and written assessments by outside experts were optional. The institution that a modern author encounters, in which every submission to a serious journal is sent to anonymous specialists whose reports shape the decision, became universal only in the second half of the twentieth century. **The first journals.** The first issue of the *Journal des sçavans* appeared in Paris in early January 1665. Henry Oldenburg, secretary of the Royal Society of London, brought a copy to the Society within days and laid the first issue of the *Philosophical Transactions* before its Council on 1 March 1665 [@fyfe2022history]. The *Transactions* was Oldenburg's private and partly commercial venture, not an organ of the Society, and he edited 136 issues until his death in 1677. Selection in this period was editorial review in the literal sense: the editor read what correspondents sent and decided what to print. **Institutional control.** In 1752 the Royal Society assumed financial and editorial responsibility for the *Transactions*. A Committee of Papers decided which communications to publish and could call on a fellow skilled in the relevant field for advice [@moxham2018prehistory]. Historians therefore often date the beginning of peer review to 1752, although antecedents reach back into the seventeenth century [@kronick1990peer]. **Written referee reports.** The practice of commissioning written reports followed in 1831–1832. Asked for ideas to reform the Society, William Whewell proposed public reports on submitted papers, modeled on the *rapporteurs* of the Paris Académie des sciences. The first jointly written reports were commissioned in December 1831, and in November 1832 the Society's president announced that no paper would be printed without a written report of its fitness [@fyfe2022history]. The Society's archive contains a continuous run of referee reports from 1832 onward, although the practice of consulting referees was not itself new [@moxham2018prehistory]. Whewell had proposed that the reports be public, but at the Royal Society referees' identities came to be kept confidential while authors were not anonymous; some journals began to anonymize authors only from the mid-1950s [@fyfe2022history; @moxham2018prehistory]. **The twentieth century.** Through the nineteenth century and much of the twentieth, external reports remained optional for journals and funding bodies [@baldwin2018autonomy]. When the editor of *Physical Review* sent a 1936 manuscript by Albert Einstein and Nathan Rosen to an anonymous referee, Einstein objected that the paper had been shown to specialists before publication and withdrew it; this was probably his first encounter with anonymous refereeing [@kennefick2005einstein]. *Nature* made external review a requirement for publication only in 1973 [@baldwin2015nature]. The phrase "peer review" itself was coined in the early 1970s [@moxham2018prehistory], and the Royal Society did not use it before 1990 [@fyfe2022history]. @baldwin2018autonomy traces the idea that refereeing is what makes science legitimate to the Cold War United States, where, under pressure on public science funding in the 1970s, scientists presented expert review as the guarantee of scientific credibility. Economics followed the same path: by the late twentieth century external refereeing was universal at the discipline's major journals, and leading economists could document that many papers later regarded as classics had been rejected along the way [@gans1994mighty]. **After the printed journal.** Four later developments complete the history and are taken up in the sections that follow. Working papers, first circulated in institutional series and then posted to online repositories, separated the communication of research from its certification (@sec-review-functions). Author anonymity became a matter of journal policy that fields resolved differently, and economics' largest society abandoned double-blind review in 2011 before announcing a randomized trial of author anonymization in 2026 (@sec-review-blinding). Data editors and data-and-code policies added verification of computational results to the review process (@sec-review-transparency). Most recently, generative artificial intelligence has lowered the cost of producing manuscripts and of checking them, and has put the scarcity of expert attention at the center of the system (@sec-review-ai-division). @tbl-review-history summarizes the milestones. | Year | Milestone | Source | |---|---|---| | 1665 | *Journal des sçavans* (January) and *Philosophical Transactions* (March) begin publication; economists debate AI-assisted review | @aea2026anonymized; @sec-review-ai-division | : Milestones in the history of journal peer review. {#tbl-review-history} ## What Journals Are For {#sec-review-functions} A journal article performs several functions at once, and the bundle has been coming apart. @ransom2026fixing, drawing on John Cochrane, describes journals as bundling three services: communication, credentialing, and archiving. Each has a different economics, and separating them explains much of the current strain on the system. **Communication.** For most of the history traced above, the journal was how research reached its readers. In economics and much of business research it no longer is. A paper is typically circulated as a working paper long before it is accepted: for articles published in 2012–2013 in leading economics journals, the median time from first submission to publication was about 35 months [@hadavand2021nber; @hadavand2024slow], and in these fields the working paper, not the article, is what circulates during those years. Working-paper output in economics rose by about a quarter at both arXiv and the NBER between the first eight months of 2025 and of 2026 [@goldsmithpinkham2026journals]. The communication function has largely moved to preprints. **Certification.** What journals still supply, and what working papers cannot, is a credible signal of quality that institutions can use without reading the work. Hiring, tenure, and promotion committees rely on it heavily. @heckman2020tyranny document the dependence in economics: in the working-paper version of their study of tenure-track hires at the top 35 U.S. departments, one publication in the five leading journals raised the rate of receiving tenure by about 80 percent relative to otherwise similar candidates, two by about 230 percent, and three by about 310 percent, and faculty surveyed ranked the number of such publications as the most important factor in tenure decisions [@heckman2019nber]. Business schools use journal lists for the same purpose (@sec-review-hierarchy). Certification is the function that makes the journal hierarchy matter, and it is the function placed under pressure when the cost of producing manuscripts falls (@sec-review-ai-division). **Archiving.** The published article is the version of record: a permanent, citable, and stable document to which corrections, expressions of concern, and retractions are attached (@sec-cred-forensics). Archiving is the least contested of the three functions and, with digital publication, the cheapest to provide. The reviewer's role differs across the three. Referees contribute little to communication, which happens before they see the paper, and nothing to archiving. Their labor is almost entirely in the service of certification, which is why the standards in @sec-review-refereeing concern whether a paper meets the journal's bar rather than how widely it should be read. ## The Publishing System {#sec-review-system} A journal is known by a single name but is several entities at once: an owner, usually a scholarly society or a university; Scholars nonetheless review for three self-interested reasons that align neatly with the field's interest. The first is **reciprocity**: peer review is a commons. Every author consumes referee labor and is expected to supply it, and a field that under-supplies reviewing degrades the screening quality of every journal in it. The second is **proximity to the frontier**: a referee reads work months or years before it appears in print, and reviewing for a strong journal is the cheapest subscription to the research frontier that exists. The third is **calibration**: nothing teaches the difference between a publishable and an unpublishable paper faster than being forced to articulate, in writing and under an editor's scrutiny, why a specific manuscript falls on one side of that line. The skills that make a good reviewer—identifying the contribution, stress-testing identification, separating fatal flaws from fixable ones—are exactly the skills that make a good author. Because the labor is invisible, it must be made visible to count. Reviewing activity can be logged on services that verify referee reports with journals (for example by forwarding the journal's acknowledgment email to a verification address), producing a citable record for promotion files and annual reviews. The mechanism matters less than the discipline of recording the work; an unrecorded review is a contribution the tenure committee never sees. ## The Editorial Pipeline A submission does not go straight to reviewers. It passes through a sequence of gates, each of which can terminate the process, and understanding that sequence demystifies both the long latencies authors experience and the points at which a paper is most likely to die. @fig-review-pipeline traces the path from submission to decision. ```{mermaid} %%| label: fig-review-pipeline %%| fig-cap: "The editorial pipeline at a top marketing journal. Submissions are screened by software for plagiarism and for duplicate or concurrent submission, the latter being a serious ethical violation because it wastes scarce referee capacity across journals. A manuscript that clears these is read by the editor (or editor-in-chief) for **suitability**: is the topic in scope, is the contribution plausibly large enough, is the execution credible on its face? A large share of submissions never survive this gate—they are **desk-rejected** without external review—which is efficient for the system but is the single most common author experience at selective journals. A suitable paper is assigned to an **area editor** or **associate editor** (AE), a domain specialist who owns the manuscript through the rest of the process. The AE selects two or three reviewers. Reviewer selection is not random: candidates are drawn from the paper's own reference list (authors of cited work are, by construction, close to the topic), from the author's suggested-reviewer list, from the AE's personal knowledge of the subfield, from candidates who declined earlier invitations and suggested alternatives, from web search, and from the publisher's reviewer database. This selection mechanism has a consequence worth stating plainly: **reviewers are chosen for topical proximity, not for statistical representativeness**, so the pool of opinions an author receives is a convenience sample of nearby experts, not a random draw from the field. Reviewers return independent written reports, and the AE **synthesizes** them into a single recommendation for the editor. Synthesis is not vote counting. A paper is not rejected because two of three reviewers were negative; it is rejected because the AE and editor, reading the reports as arguments, judge the objections dispositive. We return to why vote counting is the wrong aggregation rule in @sec-aggregating-reviews. ### How Referees Are Chosen Editors draw referees from a small number of sources: authors whose work the manuscript cites, specialists in the paper's method or data, members of the editorial board, and colleagues whose judgment the editor knows. The last two sources matter more than authors might expect. In Hamermesh's sample of referee requests at seven economics journals, nearly a third of the referees had recently published in the journal they were refereeing for, and editors relied noticeably on colleagues in their own departments [@hamermesh1994refereeing]. Referees were also disproportionately senior and highly cited: the mean referee was 16 years past the doctorate. Many journals let authors shape the pool. *Management Science* requires authors to name three associate editors and allows them to suggest five reviewers; the *Journal of Consumer Research* allows authors to suggest up to three associate editors and five reviewers and to identify reviewers they oppose; *Marketing Science* asks for a preferred senior editor, three preferred reviewers, and two preferred associate editors.[^42-title-sources] Suggestions are advisory; the editor remains free to choose referees from any source. ### Blinding {#sec-review-blinding} Review models differ in who knows whose identity. Under single-blind review the referee knows the authors but the authors do not know the referee; under double-blind (now usually called double-anonymous) review neither knows the other; under open review both identities are known. Referee anonymity became the norm at the Royal Society in the nineteenth century, whereas author anonymity is a twentieth-century innovation [@moxham2018prehistory]. Economics provides the best-known experiment and the clearest reversal. In a randomized experiment at the *American Economic Review* in the late 1980s, double-blind review produced lower acceptance rates and more critical referee reports; the effect did not differ significantly between female and male authors, and it was concentrated among authors at near-top-ranked universities and non-academic institutions [@blank1991doubleblind]. Two decades later the AEA moved its journals to single-blind review, effective July 2011, on the grounds that search engines made author anonymity increasingly ineffective and that anonymization raised administrative costs and made it harder for referees to spot conflicts of interest [@jaschik2011rejecting]. In September 2026 the AEA announced a three-year randomized trial of author-anonymized review across the *American Economic Review*, *AER: Insights*, and the four *American Economic Journals*, citing concerns about the perceived unfairness of single-blind review [@aea2026anonymized]. The evidence in @tbl-referee-evidence that prominence affects evaluations [@tomkins2017singleblind; @huber2022nobel] is the backdrop to that trial. Marketing and most of business use double-anonymous review. @tbl-review-blinding records the policies stated on the journals' official pages. | Journal | Review model (official description) | |---|---| | *Journal of Marketing*, *Journal of Marketing Research* (all AMA journals) | Double-anonymous | | *Journal of Consumer Research* | Double-anonymized | | *Marketing Science*; *Management Science* | Double-anonymous | | *Strategic Management Journal* | Double-blind | | *Journal of Finance* | Single-blind | | AEA journals (*AER*, *AER: Insights*, *AEJ*s) | Single-blind since 2011; randomized trial of author anonymization announced September 2026 | : Review models at selected journals, as described on official journal pages in 2026. Sources as in the footnote to @tbl-review-titles, plus afajof.org and the AEA announcement [@aea2026anonymized]. {#tbl-review-blinding} Double-anonymous review has a practical limit that the AEA's 2011 decision identified: when working papers are posted publicly, a referee who wishes to learn the authors' identities usually can. The policy therefore works mainly by norm. A referee at a double-anonymous journal should not search for the authors and should disclose to the editor if the authors' identity becomes known. ### Payment and Deadlines Refereeing is almost always unpaid. The exceptions are small and concentrated in economics and finance: the American Finance Association pays an honorarium of \$250 for timely, high-quality reports to the *Journal of Finance*; the *Journal of Financial Economics* has used part of its submission fee for tokens of appreciation to reviewers who deliver quality reports on time; and the *Journal of Political Economy* waives its submission fee for authors who have written three or more reports for it in the previous year.[^42-pay-sources] Experimental evidence shows that even small payments speed reports: a \$100 payment for meeting a four-week deadline shortened median review times at the *Journal of Public Economics* by about eight days beyond the effect of the shorter deadline itself [@chetty2014referees]. Requested deadlines range from about two to eight weeks. The *Journal of Public Economics* allowed 45 days before the Chetty–Saez–Sándor experiment, an *American Economic Journal* invitation reproduced by @ransom2026referee asks for a report within five weeks, and the *Journal of Marketing*'s norm, described below, is about three weeks. Observed times are close to these targets for most referees: across fields, the median reviewer completes a report about 16 days after accepting the invitation [@publons2018gspr], and in Hamermesh's economics sample half of the reports that were eventually received arrived within six weeks and three-quarters within ten [@hamermesh1994refereeing]. [^42-pay-sources]: AFA referee honoraria document (afajof.org, consulted November 2026); *Journal of Financial Economics* guide for authors (archived copy, March 2024); *Journal of Political Economy* submission instructions (archived copy, July 2025). ### The Scale of Refereeing Work {#sec-review-scale} The aggregate burden is large and unevenly distributed. @aczel2021billion estimate that peer review across all fields consumed about 131 million hours in 2020, assuming six hours per review, and that the average reviewer completes about 4.7 reviews a year. Survey data put the median time spent writing a review at five hours, and indicate that about 10 percent of reviewers perform about half of all reviews [@publons2018gspr]. Recruiting referees has become harder: editors needed 2.4 invitations per completed review in 2017, up from 1.9 in 2013 [@publons2018gspr]. The load varies over a career. Requests rise as a researcher becomes known and cited and decline after mid-career; in one economics department Hamermesh found the number of papers refereed peaked about 16 years after the doctorate, and heavily cited faculty refereed several times as many papers as the department's average [@hamermesh1994refereeing]. One economist's account gives a sense of the individual scale: about 175 referee reports written to date and 50 to 60 hours a year spent refereeing, roughly 3 to 4 percent of working time [@ransom2026fixing]. Invitations are therefore few early in a career and numerous for established scholars, whose most important refereeing skill may be declining promptly (@sec-review-refereeing). ### Decisions and Turnaround The editor's decision falls into a small set of categories. An outright **reject** ends the relationship with the journal. An **accept** is rare on a first round. The common non-terminal outcome is a **revise and resubmit** (R&R), of which two flavors must be distinguished because authors routinely confuse them. | Outcome | Treated as | Returns to | Author expectation | |---|---|---|---| | Accept | Final | Production | Rare on round 1 | | Reject | Final | — | Most common at selective journals | | Revise & resubmit (revise) | Continuation | **Same** reviewers | Address numbered points; reasonable odds | | Reject & resubmit | **New** submission | **New** reviewers | Fresh clock, fresh referees, no continuity | : First-round decision categories. The two R&R variants share a label but differ in whether the revision re-enters with the original referees or starts over. {#tbl-decisions} The distinction in @tbl-decisions is consequential. A *revise-and-resubmit* returns to the **same** reviewers, who will check whether their numbered concerns were addressed; continuity of referees rewards a disciplined, point-by-point response. A *reject-and-resubmit* is administratively a **new** paper—it resets the clock and is sent to a **new** set of reviewers—so the prior reports are guidance, not a binding contract, and the author cannot assume the new panel shares the old panel's priorities. Turnaround norms at top journals target roughly three weeks for a reviewer to return a report after accepting the invitation and on the order of two weeks for the AE to synthesize, with the full first round commonly completing within about three months. Critically, an invited reviewer should **decline promptly** if unable to serve: a slow non-answer is more damaging to an author than a fast decline, because it delays reassignment. ### Who Does What Each party to the process has a distinct job, and most failures of the process are failures of one party to do its own job or attempts to do another's. - The author's job is to submit the best paper the author can write and, after a revise-and-resubmit, to write a thoughtful response that addresses every required point and explains, with reasons, any suggestion the authors decline. - The referee's job is to give the editor impartial, concise, expert advice. The referee works for the editor, not for the authors and not for the referee's own research program (@sec-review-refereeing). - The editor's job is to decide [@berk2017referee], to explain the decision, and, when inviting a revision, to give the authors a clear direction: which referee requests are binding, which are optional, and where the referees disagree, which view the editor shares. Editors also exercise taste, the judgment about what the journal should publish that no individual report can supply. The vocabulary of recommendations is similar across journals, though the labels vary: reject, major revision, minor revision, and accept, with "revise and resubmit" used for any invitation to revise. Some journals use finer scales. The four economics journals studied by @carddellavigna2020editors ask referees to choose among seven categories, from "definitely reject" to "accept". Their data show how severe referees are. The published criteria at JM reduce to three properties a publishable article must simultaneously possess. > A publishable article offers **new knowledge**, addresses **real-world marketing > topics and problems** of relevance to identifiable stakeholders, and exhibits > **validity**—a good approximation of the truth. These three—novelty, relevance, validity—are not independently sufficient. A methodologically flawless paper that tells the field nothing new fails on novelty; a novel and rigorous paper about a phenomenon no stakeholder cares about fails on relevance; a novel and important paper whose inference does not survive scrutiny fails on validity, which is usually fatal because validity, unlike novelty or relevance, cannot be repaired by reframing. Much of what a reviewer does is to locate which of these three a paper is weakest on and judge whether the weakness is fixable within a revision cycle. ## The Process Reviewers Are Held To The author is not the only party under evaluation; the **review itself** is held to standards, and an AE who receives a careless or unfair report will discount it. @tbl-review-standards collects the properties a competent review must satisfy. These are obligations on the referee, not on the manuscript. | Standard | What it requires of the reviewer | |---|---| | Fairness | Judge the paper the authors wrote, against its stated objective | | Competence | Possess reasonable domain knowledge for the claims at issue | | Independence | Disclose and recuse on conflicts of interest | | Consistency | Weigh interest, empirical rigor, conceptual rigor, relevance, constructiveness, and tolerance for risk | | Non-vote-counting | Supply arguments, not a verdict count, for the AE to weigh | | Responsibility | Respect the original objective, explain fatal flaws explicitly, preserve confidentiality | | Timeliness | Reviewers ~3 weeks post-acceptance; AEs ~2 weeks to synthesize | | Roadmap | Tell the author what a successful revision would look like | : Standards the review process imposes on reviewers (JM editorial practice). {#tbl-review-standards} Two of these deserve emphasis because they are the most often violated. **Consistency** means a reviewer should reward **risk-taking**: a paper that attempts something hard and important and partly succeeds can be a larger contribution than a paper that executes a small, safe question flawlessly, and a review that mechanically penalizes ambition starves the field of its most valuable submissions. **Responsibility** means that when a reviewer believes a flaw is fatal, the report must *explain why*, in enough detail that the author understands the objection rather than merely the verdict; an unexplained rejection is a failure of the reviewer, not a service to the field. The combination of these standards with a **roadmap**—an explicit statement of what a successful revision would contain—is what converts a review from a judgment into a constructive instrument. ## Anatomy of a Referee Report A good report is short, numbered, and organized so the AE can extract a recommendation and the author can extract a to-do list. The conventional length is about two single-spaced pages, and comments are **numbered** so that author and editor can reference them precisely in correspondence. @fig-report-structure shows the canonical structure, which mirrors the three-paragraph template many editors recommend: contextualize, evaluate, then enumerate issues. ```{mermaid} %%| label: fig-report-structure %%| fig-cap: "Canonical structure of a referee report. Restating the paper's thesis is not a courtesy; it lets the author and editor verify that the reviewer understood the contribution before critiquing it, and a reviewer who cannot summarize the paper accurately has forfeited the authority to reject it. The middle of the report **evaluates** the work along the dimensions the field cares about: is the paper well written, interesting, and important; are the methods, data, and design appropriate; and—the decisive empirical question—**does the data support the findings**? The body then enumerates issues, and the most useful reports separate the **major** comments (factual errors, invalid arguments, identification problems, claims unsupported by the evidence) from **minor** ones (exposition, length relative to the journal's norms, missing references), and pair each major objection with a **path to improvement** wherever one exists. The distinction between major and minor is not cosmetic. An AE reading three reports needs to know which objections are dispositive and which are polish, and a report that buries a fatal identification problem in a list of typographical corrections has failed to communicate its own conclusion. The closing of a strong report is the roadmap from @tbl-review-standards: a concrete statement of what the authors would have to demonstrate for the reviewer to change a negative recommendation to a positive one. @sec-review-refereeing develops each of these elements in full. ## Refereeing a Paper {#sec-review-refereeing} The preceding sections describe the report as an object. This section treats refereeing as a task: a sequence of decisions that begins when an invitation arrives and ends, often more than a year later, when a revised manuscript is accepted or rejected. The treatment draws principally on the guidance that @berk2017referee distilled from correspondence with former editors of the *American Economic Review*, the *Journal of Political Economy*, the *Quarterly Journal of Economics*, *Econometrica*, the *Review of Economic Studies*, and the *Journal of Financial Economics*, together with their longer working-paper guide [@berk2015referee] and a recent teaching adaptation of both [@ransom2026referee]. Those sources come from economics and finance. The principles transfer to marketing without modification, and where marketing practice differs the difference is noted. The prescriptions are then tied to the empirical literature on how referees actually behave, because several of the most important rules exist to counteract documented failure modes rather than as matters of taste. ### The Division of Labor The referee is an expert adviser. The referee does not make the publication decision; the editor does, and the editor communicates it to the authors. The invitation letter at most journals says as much: the editor requests the referee's *advice* on a manuscript. Three consequences follow from this division of labor, and most of the guidance in this section is an elaboration of one of them. First, the report must be useful to a decision-maker who is frequently not a specialist in the paper's subfield. An assertion that a paper is unimportant, or that its results are wrong, is informative to such an editor only when it is accompanied by an argument the editor can evaluate. Second, every comment in a report belongs to one of three categories, and the referee must say which [@berk2017referee; @ransom2026referee]. @tbl-referee-comment-bins sets them out. The first category contains requirements: problems that render the paper unpublishable in its current form and that must be resolved before the referee would recommend acceptance. These are advice to the editor. The second contains suggestions: changes that would improve the paper but do not bear on whether it is publishable. These are advice to the authors, and the authors are free to decline them. The third category is empty by construction. It consists of demands that do not affect publishability but are nonetheless presented as conditions of acceptance, and a referee should not make them. | Category | Content | Addressed to | Burden of justification | Binding on a revision? | |---|---|---|---|---| | Requirement | A problem that makes the paper unpublishable now but is correctable | Editor (and authors) | A scientifically convincing argument | Yes: if resolved, the referee should recommend publication | | Ground for rejection | A problem unlikely to be correctable within one round, or an insufficient contribution | Editor | A scientifically convincing argument | Not applicable | | Suggestion | An improvement or extension that does not affect publishability | Authors | None beyond a brief rationale | No: authors may decline without penalty | | Out of bounds | A demand presented as required although it does not affect publishability | — | — | Should not be made | : The categories of referee comments. Where reasonable scholars could disagree about exposition, emphasis, or the inclusion of secondary analyses, the decision rests with the authors, whose names appear on the article [@berk2017referee]. The referee is neither a coauthor who rewrites the paper, nor a research director who steers an unpublishable paper toward publishability over several rounds, nor an enforcer who ensures that the referee's own work is cited [@ransom2026referee]. @bedeian2004peer, writing about management journals, frames the same point as the preservation of the authorial voice against the accumulated preferences of referees and editors. ### What Is Known About Refereeing The rules of good refereeing would be matters of etiquette if referees were reliable instruments. Each entry reports only what the cited study establishes; settings outside marketing are noted because no comparable marketing-journal data are public. {#tbl-referee-evidence} Four conclusions follow from the table, and each motivates a rule developed below. The first is that referee judgments are noisy. The low reliability documented by @cicchetti1991reliability, @bornmann2010reliability, and @welch2014referee is the empirical counterpart of the rater-effect terms in the measurement model of @sec-aggregating-reviews. @berk2017referee add that recommendations at a major finance conference were correlated at only 0.28, and @gilliland1997reviewer report similar disagreement for submissions to the *Journal of Applied Psychology*. A referee who knows this will state recommendations with appropriate humility and support them with arguments that the editor can weigh independently of the verdict. The second is that referees miss most errors. In both *BMJ* trials, the typical reviewer found fewer than one-third of the major problems deliberately planted in a paper [@godlee1998blinding; @schroter2008errors]. Unstructured reading is therefore an unreliable method of verification, which motivates the structured reading protocol below. The third is that referee judgments are not independent of who wrote the paper or what it found. Prominence [@tomkins2017singleblind; @huber2022nobel], network proximity [@teplitskiy2018network], and agreement with the referee's prior views [@mahoney1977prejudices] all move evaluations of identical work. The evidence on gender is more nuanced and depends on the benchmark. @card2020gender find that male and female referees assess female-authored papers similarly relative to male-authored papers, but that female-authored papers receive about 25 percent more citations than observably similar male-authored papers holding referee evaluations fixed; on a citation benchmark, the system as a whole sets a higher bar for female authors. @squazzoni2021gender, comparing outcomes directly across 145 journals, find that manuscripts with female authors were treated, if anything, more favorably. A referee cannot resolve this debate but can take the mechanism seriously: evaluations should rest on the content of the manuscript, assessed against criteria fixed before the referee forms a view of the authors. The fourth is that referees do add value and that delays are concentrated. Referee comments predict later citations [@laband1990valueadded], and editors rely on referee recommendations because they carry information [@carddellavigna2020editors]. Most referees respond quickly; the long delays that authors experience come disproportionately from a small group who accept an assignment and then neither report nor withdraw [@hamermesh1994refereeing]. Simple policies such as shorter deadlines shorten review times without reducing report quality [@chetty2014referees]. The aggregate slowdown of publication in economics is attributed mainly to more extensive revision demands rather than to slower referees [@ellison2002slowdown], and @hadavand2024slow find that much of the remaining lag reflects the time authors take to revise. The referee's leverage over total delay therefore lies less in the speed of the first report than in the scope of what the report requires. ### Before Accepting the Invitation An invitation typically contains the title, the abstract, and often the manuscript, a requested deadline, and a request to disclose conflicts of interest. The referee should decide promptly. An invitation declined within a day or two, with suggestions of alternative referees, costs the author almost nothing; an invitation accepted and then neglected can hold a paper for months [@hamermesh1994refereeing; @berk2017referee]. @fig-referee-invitation lays out the questions to resolve before accepting. ```{mermaid} %%| label: fig-referee-invitation %%| fig-cap: "Questions to resolve before accepting a referee invitation.
