Conflicts also arise from the research itself: the referee has competing work in progress, the manuscript contradicts or corrects the referee's own published work, or the referee has had a prior dispute with an author. In each case the editor, not the referee, decides whether the referee should proceed. The guidance issued by the Committee on Publication Ethics treats disclosure and confidentiality as the two core obligations of a reviewer [@cope2013reviewers]. **Competence and fit.** A referee who knows little about the relevant literature should ask the editor whether the assignment is a mistake. The editor may have intended the referee to evaluate one component, such as the empirical design of a paper that also contains a theoretical model, and knowing this focuses the report [@berk2017referee]. @shugan2007secrets argues from the editor's side that, for many submissions, some reviewers should evaluate the procedures while others evaluate the contribution, which is a further reason to clarify the role before starting. **Prior review.** If the referee has already reviewed the manuscript for another journal, the editor should be told immediately. Some editors prefer a fresh reader; others value a referee who can assess whether the paper has improved. The choice belongs to the editor [@berk2017referee]. **Anonymity.** A referee who has discussed the paper at a conference or in correspondence may be unable to write a report that the authors would not recognize. Declining is reasonable in that case; alternatively, the referee can alert the editor and, if asked, provide a confidential letter without a report. Even then, a negative assessment must be supported by an argument the editor can evaluate [@berk2017referee]. **Confidentiality.** A manuscript under review is a confidential document. It may not be shared, cited, or used to advance the referee's own work, and it may not be uploaded to an external tool unless the journal's policy expressly permits it [@cope2013reviewers; @ransom2026referee]. The constraint on artificial-intelligence tools is discussed in @sec-cred-ai-review and below. A referee who wishes to involve a doctoral student or colleague in the review must first obtain the editor's permission. ### Reading the Manuscript Because unaided reading misses most errors [@godlee1998blinding; @schroter2008errors], the reading itself should be structured. The following three-pass protocol is a synthesis written for this chapter rather than a procedure prescribed by any one source; it organizes the questions that the cited guides pose. The first pass establishes what the paper claims. The referee reads the abstract, introduction, conclusion, and principal exhibits, and then writes, without looking back at the text, a one-paragraph summary of the research question, the claimed contribution, and the evidence offered for it. If the referee cannot write that paragraph, the paper has an exposition problem that may itself be serious; if the referee can, the paragraph becomes the opening of the report. At the end of the first pass the referee should record a provisional view of importance, because that view will be revised and the revision is itself informative. The second pass tests the core argument. For a theoretical paper this means working through the central propositions and their proofs. For an empirical paper it means asking, for each headline estimate, what variation identifies it, what the main threats to that identification are, and whether the paper's own evidence addresses them. The marketing-specific version of these questions draws on earlier chapters: whether the measured variables correspond to the constructs the theory names (@sec-construct-vs-variable, @sec-measurement-scales), whether the design supports a causal reading (@sec-causal-inference), and whether the paper's claims match the strength of its evidence (@sec-scientific-writing). The second pass is where most fatal problems are found. The third pass covers details: robustness analyses, appendices, the data description, and, where one is provided, the replication package (@sec-review-transparency). Details matter in proportion to their consequence for the headline claims. An error in a robustness table that the conclusion does not depend on is a minor comment; an error in the construction of the main dependent variable is not. Two disciplines govern all three passes. The referee should evaluate the paper the authors wrote, against the objective they set, rather than the paper the referee would have written. And the referee should treat a surprising result as a reason to request evidence rather than as evidence of error. @berk2017referee put the second point in Bayesian terms: a result with a low prior probability warrants more and better evidence before it is believed, but the appropriate response is to ask for that evidence, and, if the authors supply it, to leave further updating to subsequent research. A referee who discounts evidence because it is unexpected is exhibiting the confirmatory bias that @mahoney1977prejudices documented. ### Assessing Importance Importance is the hardest judgment a referee makes and the most subjective [@berk2017referee]. Selective journals receive far more correct papers than they can publish; in the top five economics journals the acceptance rate fell from about 15 percent in the late 1970s to about 6 percent by 2012, and annual submissions nearly doubled between 1990 and 2012 [@carddellavigna2013ninefacts]. The question is therefore rarely whether a paper is correct. It is whether the paper addresses a question of sufficiently broad interest and makes a sufficient advance over existing work to justify publication in this journal. Because the judgment is subjective, the report must make it contestable. A statement that the contribution is "incremental" or "not of broad interest" is useful to the editor only when it identifies the closest prior work, explains what the manuscript adds to it, and says why that addition falls short of the journal's standard. The same discipline applies in the positive direction. @berk2017referee caution that ambitious papers are more likely to have loose ends, and that referees and editors therefore tend to undervalue them relative to safe papers that address small questions without blemish. Their proposed test is whether, flaws included, the referee would have been pleased to have written the paper. If the flaws do not invalidate the contribution and the contribution is important, the appropriate recommendation is to publish. In marketing, the corresponding risk is that methodological sophistication is rewarded over the substance of the question [@lehmann2011], and that the standards referees apply diverge from what the field's external audiences need [@reibstein2009losing]. A referee who assesses importance explicitly, rather than letting the absence of blemishes stand in for it, counteracts both tendencies. ### Assessing Validity A fatal problem is one that invalidates the paper's central claim and is unlikely to be correctable within one round of revision. To support a recommendation of rejection on validity grounds, the referee must provide a scientifically based argument that the editor can evaluate. A hunch is not sufficient [@berk2017referee; @ransom2026referee]. For a theoretical paper, a referee who does not believe a result should locate the error in the proof or construct a counterexample to the claim. If the authors show that the counterexample is itself mistaken, the proposition stands, and the referee may not retreat into generalized skepticism. The referee may legitimately ask the authors to reconcile the result with existing findings or to explain how much it depends on nonstandard assumptions, while recognizing that the paper may be right and the prior literature wrong. For an empirical paper, the statement that results "do not pass the smell test" is equally insufficient. The referee should identify the specific mechanism by which the result could be spurious (an omitted confounder, a selection process, a measurement artifact, a specification search) and request the specific analysis that would distinguish that mechanism from the authors' interpretation. A request framed in this way is falsifiable: the authors can run the analysis, and the result either supports or undermines the claim. Each of the failure modes catalogued in @sec-credibility, from forking paths to implausibly uniform data, can be converted into a request of this kind. ### Which Requests Are Required: A Decision-Theoretic Criterion {#sec-review-pivotal} The distinction between requirements and suggestions is, according to @berk2017referee, the point on which referees most often fail, and the failure is costly. Unlabeled secondary comments are coercive in practice, because few authors will risk rejection at a top journal to omit a robustness check that a referee mentioned [@berk2017referee]. The accumulation of such requests is the mechanism behind the lengthening of papers and review cycles documented by @ellison2002slowdown and @carddellavigna2013ninefacts. @ellison2002qr models this as a gradual drift in the norms that weight a paper's main idea ($q$) against other aspects of quality ($r$). @hirshleifer2015cosmetic models it as signal-jamming: when an editor cannot distinguish a serious flaw from a blemish, referees demand the repair of blemishes to appear skilled, editors accede, and papers that cannot be made blemish-free, which disproportionately include innovative papers and replications, are blocked. @spiegel2012reviewing argues that the underlying problem is the profession's inability to declare a paper good enough. This chapter offers a simple criterion that makes the distinction operational. Let $V \in \{0, 1\}$ indicate whether the paper's central claim is valid and let $p = \Pr(V = 1)$ be the referee's current belief. Suppose that publishing a valid paper yields a benefit normalized to 1, publishing an invalid one imposes a loss $L$, and rejection yields 0. Publication is then warranted when $$ p - (1 - p) L \ge 0 \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad p \ge \tau \equiv \frac{L}{1 + L}. $$ {#eq-referee-threshold} A requested analysis $k$ produces a pass with probability $a_k$ if the claim is valid and $b_k$ if it is not, so after a pass the referee's belief becomes $$ p^{+}_k = \frac{p\, a_k}{p\, a_k + (1 - p)\, b_k}, \qquad p^{-}_k = \frac{p\,(1 - a_k)}{p\,(1 - a_k) + (1 - p)(1 - b_k)} $$ {#eq-referee-posterior} after a pass or a failure respectively. Call request $k$ *pivotal* if at least one of its outcomes moves the belief across the threshold, so that the recommendation would change: $p < \tau \le p^{+}_k$ or $p^{-}_k < \tau \le p$. The criterion is then: > A request belongs among the requirements only if it is pivotal and its expected > value of information exceeds the cost it imposes on the authors. A request that is > not pivotal can be at most a suggestion. The expected value of information is the improvement in the expected payoff of the publication decision from observing the outcome before deciding, $$ \text{VOI}_k = \Pr(\text{pass})\,\max\{0,\, v(p^{+}_k)\} + \Pr(\text{fail})\,\max\{0,\, v(p^{-}_k)\} - \max\{0,\, v(p)\}, $$ {#eq-referee-voi} with $v(x) = x - (1 - x)L$ and $\Pr(\text{pass}) = p\,a_k + (1 - p)\,b_k$. A non-pivotal request has $\text{VOI}_k = 0$ by construction, whatever its cost. The criterion formalizes the advice of @berk2017referee that a request must have positive net present value, given that the authors bear its cost, and it identifies the requests that signal-jamming produces: analyses whose outcomes could not change any reader's assessment of the claim. The calculation below illustrates the criterion. It is a stylized example written for this section, with hypothetical numbers. A referee believes with probability 0.6 that an empirical paper's central effect is causal and requires 0.75 before recommending publication ($L = 3$). Three requests are under consideration: a placebo test that a causal effect should pass and a confounded one should usually fail; re-estimation with an alternative clustering of standard errors, which a confounded effect would also usually survive; and the addition of one further year to a long, hand-collected panel, which would almost always leave the estimate unchanged whether or not it is causal. ::: {#tbl-referee-voi .cell layout-align="center" tbl-cap='Pivotality and expected value of information for three hypothetical referee requests (stylized example). Prior belief p = 0.6 that the central claim is valid; publication threshold tau = 0.75 (L = 3). Only the placebo test can move the referee across the threshold, so only it can be a requirement; the other two are at most suggestions.'} ```{.r .cell-code} # Stylized illustration written for this section; the numbers are hypothetical. p <- 0.60 # referee's current belief that the central claim is valid L <- 3 # loss from publishing an invalid paper (benefit of a valid one = 1) tau <- L / (1 + L) # publication threshold, eq-referee-threshold v <- function(x) x - (1 - x) * L # expected payoff of publishing at belief x requests <- data.frame( request = c("Placebo test", "Alternative clustering", "One more year of data"), a = c(0.95, 0.90, 0.97), # Pr(pass | claim valid) b = c(0.30, 0.60, 0.90) # Pr(pass | claim invalid) ) with(requests, { pass <- p * a + (1 - p) * b p_pass <- p * a / pass # eq-referee-posterior p_fail <- p * (1 - a) / (1 - pass) pivotal <- (p < tau & p_pass >= tau) | (p >= tau & p_fail < tau) voi <- pass * pmax(0, v(p_pass)) + (1 - pass) * pmax(0, v(p_fail)) - max(0, v(p)) # eq-referee-voi data.frame(Request = request, `Pr(pass)` = round(pass, 3), `Belief after pass` = round(p_pass, 3), `Belief after fail` = round(p_fail, 3), Pivotal = ifelse(pivotal, "yes", "no"), VOI = round(voi, 3), check.names = FALSE) }) |> knitr::kable() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} |Request | Pr(pass)| Belief after pass| Belief after fail|Pivotal | VOI| |:----------------------|--------:|-----------------:|-----------------:|:-------|----:| |Placebo test | 0.690| 0.826| 0.097|yes | 0.21| |Alternative clustering | 0.780| 0.692| 0.273|no | 0.00| |One more year of data | 0.942| 0.618| 0.310|no | 0.00| ::: ::: The placebo test can raise the referee's belief to about 0.83, above the threshold, so it is pivotal and has positive value; it is a legitimate requirement, provided its cost to the authors is commensurate. The alternative clustering raises the belief only to about 0.69 even if it passes. Because the recommendation would not change, it should at most be offered as a suggestion, however routine it may seem to request. The extra year of data is so weakly diagnostic that neither outcome moves the belief across the threshold, and its cost to the authors is high; it should not be requested at all. @berk2017referee report an editor's account of almost exactly this case: a referee insisted that a hand-collected panel of 19 years be extended to 20, and the editor instructed the authors to ignore the request. The criterion has two further implications. A referee whose belief already exceeds the threshold should recommend acceptance unless some feasible analysis could reveal the claim to be invalid, and should otherwise list further analyses as suggestions. And because the criterion depends on the referee's own prior and threshold, it does not remove judgment from refereeing. It requires the referee to make that judgment explicit, which is what allows the editor to evaluate it. Large language models and coding agents have lowered the cost of running one more specification [@ransom2026referee], but the criterion turns on whether an analysis is informative, not on whether it is cheap, so lower costs do not make non-pivotal requests any more appropriate. ### Writing the Report A referee submits two documents: a report, which is sent to the authors, and a confidential letter to the editor. The report's purpose is to help the editor decide whether to publish; helping the authors improve the paper is a valuable secondary purpose, but it must not interfere with the first [@berk2017referee]. The following structure serves both. 1. **Summary.** One paragraph stating the research question, the claimed contribution, and the line of reasoning, in the referee's own words. It shows the authors and the editor that the referee understood the paper. 2. **Assessment of importance.** The referee's view of the contribution relative to the closest prior work, with the reasons for it. 3. **Assessment of validity.** Whether the evidence supports the central claims. 4. **Essential concerns.** A numbered list of the requirements and, where applicable, the grounds for rejection, each with its supporting argument and, where one exists, a concrete path to resolution. 5. **Suggestions.** A separately numbered list of optional improvements, labeled as such. 6. **Minor points.** Errors of fact, notation, or reference that the authors can correct quickly, collected at the end where the editor can skip them. Numbering is a small matter with a large effect on the efficiency of the process, because it lets authors, referees, and editors refer to specific comments across rounds. @berk2017referee recommend separate numbering for essential concerns and suggestions, so that no reader can mistake one for the other. The skeleton below implements the structure. ```text Report on Manuscript [number]: "[title]" Summary [One paragraph: question, claimed contribution, evidence, main findings.] Assessment [Two or three paragraphs: importance relative to the closest prior work; whether the evidence supports the central claims; the overall judgment, stated consistently with the confidential recommendation.] Essential concerns (must be resolved for the paper to be publishable) E1. [Problem.] [Why it undermines a specific claim.] [What analysis or argument would resolve it, and what result would do so.] E2. ... Suggestions (optional; the authors may decline without consequence) S1. [Improvement and brief rationale.] S2. ... Minor points M1. [Page/equation/table reference and correction.] ``` **Length.** The report is not a record of everything the referee thought while reading. @berk2017referee report an editor's view that two to three pages suffice unless the issues are highly technical and that a ten-page report is punitive; they stop short of endorsing a fixed length but observe that brief reports often contain more important content than lengthy ones. When a paper is far below the journal's standard, a one-page report returned within a week serves everyone better than an exhaustive analysis of an obvious conclusion: if the editor disagrees, another referee can be engaged without delay [@berk2017referee; @ransom2026referee]. If the justification for a quick rejection proves hard to write, the paper may not be as far below the standard as it first appeared. **Exposition.** The referee is not a copyeditor [@ransom2026referee]. Writing so poor that the paper cannot be understood is a legitimate ground for rejection, because the contribution cannot be evaluated. When an important idea is obscured by poor writing, the referee can suggest to the editor that the authors withdraw and resubmit after revision [@ransom2026referee]. Below that level, comments on style belong among the suggestions. **Tone.** The report should address the substance of the paper in neutral language. It should not ascribe motives to the authors, insult them, or use emotional or accusatory language; a report that is uniformly negative in tone weakens its own critical points [@berk2017referee]. A referee who suspects intellectual dishonesty should state the relevant facts without speculating about intent and should raise the concern in the letter to the editor, who decides whether to put it to the authors. A useful final test is the one @ransom2026referee calls the golden rule of reviewing: whether the referee would regard the report as fair if it had been written about the referee's own paper. ### The Letter to the Editor The confidential letter should be short and should not repeat the report. It should convey three things [@berk2017referee]: the broad interest and importance of the contribution relative to existing work, explained for an editor who may not be a specialist; whether the analysis is convincing; and a frank assessment of whether the paper is publishable as it stands or is likely to become publishable after one round of revision. The referee should be decisive. The recommendation scale (reject, major revision, minor revision, accept, with variations across journals) asks for a judgment, and a recommendation to revise that merely defers the judgment is not helpful [@ransom2026referee]. Uncertainty belongs in the explanation, not in the recommendation. A referee who is confident about the empirical design but not about a theoretical component should say so and may suggest a second referee, with names and with a description of what that referee should examine; such a suggestion should not substitute for the work of reaching a view [@berk2017referee]. The letter and the report must tell the same story. @berk2017referee recount a case in which a report praised a paper in the strongest terms while the referee recommended rejection in the confidential channel; when the editor rejected the paper, the author appealed by quoting the report. Because editors are free to disclose recommendations to authors, the tone of the report should never imply a recommendation more favorable than the one the referee has made. ### The Revise-and-Resubmit Contract A recommendation to revise and resubmit makes three statements at once: that the paper is important enough for the journal, that it currently has problems that make it unpublishable, and that those problems are correctable [@berk2017referee]. It is also an implicit contract with the authors, who will invest months in the revision on the understanding that if they resolve the stated requirements, the referee will recommend publication. Recommending a revision is therefore a serious commitment and should not be used to postpone a decision [@ransom2026referee]. The contract has three consequences for later rounds. First, the referee should do the substantive work in the first round. A concern that could have been raised in the first report but is raised only in the second imposes the full cost of a wasted round on the authors and places the editor in a difficult position; if it happens, the referee should acknowledge the oversight to the editor and the authors [@berk2017referee]. Second, the referee should not move the goalposts. A new list of requests in the second round, or a change of view about the contribution unrelated to the authors' response, breaches the contract. Third, the referee may not penalize the authors for declining a suggestion. @tbl-referee-rounds summarizes the resulting norms. | First-round report | Authors' response | Referee's next step | |---|---|---| | Paper publishable subject to one required analysis | Run the analysis; the result holds | Recommend acceptance | | Paper publishable; several suggestions offered | Decline the suggestions with reasons | Recommend acceptance | | Several problems, some labeled essential | Resolve the essential problems but not the others | Recommend acceptance | | Several problems, some labeled essential | Resolve the essential problems; the revision itself reveals a new, unforeseeable issue | Raise the new issue, explain why it could not have been raised earlier, and keep the request narrow | | Several problems, some labeled essential | Resolve only some of the essential problems | Consider, with the editor, whether a further round is warranted before recommending rejection | : Norms for the second round of a revise-and-resubmit. The first three rows follow @ransom2026referee; the last two follow @berk2017referee. {#tbl-referee-rounds} The second-round report is accordingly shorter than the first. It should take each essential concern in turn, state whether the response resolves it, and, if it does not, explain specifically why. On this view a revise-and-resubmit should normally reach a final decision after one round [@berk2017referee]. @hadavand2024slow find that, at top economics journals, additional rounds of resubmission are associated with more citations, but that, conditional on resubmission, longer delays are not. The association with impact lies in the substance of revision, not in the time it consumes, which is a further reason to state every requirement in the first report. ### Ethics Beyond disclosure and confidentiality, three ethical obligations are specific to the referee's position. The first prohibits using the review to advance the referee's own work. Requests that the authors cite the referee's papers, when those papers are not necessary to the argument, are a misuse of the review [@berk2017referee]. So is delaying a report to gain priority for competing work. @berk2017referee describe an editor who, after a referee delayed a report and then posted a competing paper, alerted the editors of other leading journals. The second governs ideas obtained from the manuscript. If the paper has not been publicly distributed, the referee cannot work on the topic in a way that relies on it, because the referee is not in a position to cite it properly. If it has been publicly distributed, the referee may work on the same topic, as anyone may, provided the work cites the manuscript as prior work; if that decision is made while the review is in progress, the editor must be told immediately [@berk2017referee]. The third concerns misconduct by the authors. A referee who discovers that a manuscript duplicates one under review elsewhere, or contains plagiarized material, should inform the editor promptly and confine the communication to the facts [@berk2017referee; @ransom2026referee]. Investigation is the editor's responsibility, and the institutional processes for handling it are described in @sec-cred-forensics. **Artificial-intelligence tools.** The referee must follow the journal's policy on artificial intelligence and must not upload a manuscript to a tool the policy does not permit [@ransom2026referee]; the reasons, and the controversy over whether models should be built into review itself, are set out in @sec-cred-ai-review. The evidence on the quality of model-generated feedback is mixed in a way that matters for referees. In a prospective study of 308 researchers who received GPT-4-generated feedback on their own papers, 57.4 percent found it helpful or very helpful and 82.4 percent found it more beneficial than feedback from at least some human reviewers, but the authors also document limitations and conclude that expert human review should remain the foundation of the process [@liang2024llmfeedback]. Model output can therefore inform an author's revision before submission. It cannot replace the referee's own judgment, and a referee who signs a report is responsible for every statement in it. ### Refereeing in Marketing Marketing journals share the editorial structure of @fig-review-pipeline, with an area or associate editor who selects referees, reads their reports, and writes a synthesis for the editor. That structure changes the audience of the report but not its principles: the associate editor is often closer to the subfield than an economics editor would be, which raises rather than lowers the premium on reports that separate essential concerns from suggestions, because the synthesis must reconcile several referees' lists into a single set of requirements. @shugan2007secrets, writing as editor of *Marketing Science*, argues that reviewers should not micromanage revisions, a position that coincides with the treatment of suggestions above. Marketing also spans methodological traditions with different characteristic failure modes, and a referee evaluating work outside the referee's own tradition should calibrate what counts as fatal. @tbl-referee-genres, written for this chapter, gives examples by genre. It is a starting point for the second reading pass, not an exhaustive checklist, and it should be read alongside the genre-specific templates in @sec-scientific-writing. | Genre | Typically fatal if uncorrectable | Typically fixable or optional | |---|---|---| | Behavioral experiments | Manipulation that does not isolate the construct; confounded conditions; effect contingent on undisclosed exclusions or analyses | Additional mediators or moderators; further replications of an already well-powered effect | | Archival and econometric studies | Identifying variation that is plausibly confounded, with no design that addresses it; outcome or treatment mismeasured in a way that drives the result | Alternative standard errors or specifications that cannot change the conclusion; extended samples with no reason to expect a different answer | | Structural and analytical models | Results that depend on an assumption contradicted by the data or by the institutional setting; parameters not identified from the data used | Additional counterfactuals; generalizations of the model that leave its main mechanism unchanged | | Machine learning and text analysis | Leakage between training and evaluation data; a measure not validated against the construct it is claimed to capture | Comparison with further baseline models; additional hyperparameter searches | | Survey and scale development | Measures lacking construct validity or invariance across the groups being compared | Additional validity evidence for an already established scale | : Examples of fatal and fixable problems by research genre, written for this chapter. "Fatal" means fatal if it cannot be corrected within one round; whether a given problem is correctable is itself part of the referee's judgment. {#tbl-referee-genres} ### Learning to Referee Formal training appears to do little for error detection: short training courses had only small effects in the *BMJ* trial [@schroter2008errors]. Referees improve mainly through practice and comparison. Most editorial systems allow a referee, once a decision has been made, to read the other referees' reports and the decision letter [@ransom2026referee]; reading them, and asking what the other referees saw that one missed, is the closest a referee comes to feedback on the quality of a report. A doctoral student can gain similar experience by drafting a report alongside an adviser, provided the editor has approved the student's involvement. The resulting report should be the adviser's responsibility and should be submitted with the editor's knowledge of the student's role. The section closes with a checklist that condenses its guidance. 1. Resolve conflicts, competence, timing, prior review, and anonymity before accepting, and decline promptly if necessary. 2. Follow the journal's policies on confidentiality and artificial intelligence. 3. Read in three passes: the claims, the core argument, and the details. 4. Open the report with a summary in your own words, then assess importance and validity. 5. Support every judgment that bears on publishability with an argument the editor can evaluate; a hunch is not an argument. 6. Classify every request as a requirement or a suggestion, number the two lists separately, and require only pivotal requests whose value exceeds their cost. 7. Do not copyedit, and do not make work. 8. Write in neutral language, and confine any concern about misconduct to the facts and to the letter to the editor. 9. Make the letter to the editor short and decisive, and consistent with the report. 10. Do the substantive work in the first round, and honor the revise-and-resubmit contract in the second. ## Reviewing as Measurement {#sec-aggregating-reviews} Peer review is, formally, a **measurement** procedure: several raters observe the same object (the manuscript) and emit ordinal judgments, and the system aggregates those judgments into a decision. Viewing it this way makes precise why vote counting is the wrong aggregation rule and why even a well-run process is noisy. Let a manuscript $i$ have an unobserved latent quality $q_i \in \mathbb{R}$. Reviewer $j$ does not observe $q_i$; she observes a noisy signal and reports a rating $$ r_{ij} = q_i + b_j + \varepsilon_{ij}, $$ {#eq-rating-model} where $b_j$ is reviewer $j$'s **systematic leniency or severity** (a fixed rater effect) and $\varepsilon_{ij}$ is idiosyncratic noise with variance $\sigma^2_\varepsilon$. Equation @eq-rating-model is the linear measurement model that underlies every reliability statistic below. Two features of real review panels map directly onto its terms. First, reviewers differ in **severity** $b_j$—some referees reject almost everything—so a paper's fate depends partly on the luck of the draw in @fig-review-pipeline. Second, because reviewers are selected for topical proximity rather than at random, their errors $\varepsilon_{ij}$ need not be independent: two referees from the same methodological camp may share a blind spot, violating the independence that naive aggregation assumes. This is precisely why synthesis is not **vote counting**. Under @eq-rating-model, the AE's task is to estimate $q_i$ from the reports, and a count of "rejects" throws away exactly the information that distinguishes a severe reviewer's reflexive negativity ($b_j \ll 0$) from a substantive, dispositive objection (a genuinely low $q_i$). A reasoned synthesis reads the *arguments*—the content of $\varepsilon_{ij}$, in effect—and down-weights severity that is not backed by a defensible flaw. The formal model thus rationalizes the editorial insistence that recommendations carry arguments rather than verdicts. ### Quantifying Agreement How much do reviewers actually agree? For **continuous or quasi-continuous** ratings, the natural summary is the **intraclass correlation coefficient** (ICC), the share of total rating variance attributable to true between-manuscript differences rather than to rater effects and noise [@Shrout_1979]. Under @eq-rating-model with manuscript variance $\sigma^2_q$, the single-rater reliability is $$ \text{ICC} = \frac{\sigma^2_q}{\sigma^2_q + \sigma^2_b + \sigma^2_\varepsilon}, $$ {#eq-icc} which falls toward zero as rater severity ($\sigma^2_b$) and idiosyncratic noise ($\sigma^2_\varepsilon$) swamp the genuine quality signal. Equation @eq-icc also explains why journals assign **multiple** reviewers: averaging $m$ independent reports reduces the noise term to $\sigma^2_\varepsilon/m$, so the reliability of the *mean* rating rises with the panel size—the Spearman–Brown logic—provided the errors really are independent, which the selection mechanism above puts in doubt. For **categorical** verdicts (accept / R&R / reject), agreement is measured by **Cohen's $\kappa$**, which corrects the raw proportion of agreement for the agreement expected by chance [@Cohen_1960]. With observed agreement $p_o$ and chance agreement $p_e$, $$ \kappa = \frac{p_o - p_e}{1 - p_e}, $$ {#eq-42-kappa} so $\kappa = 1$ denotes perfect agreement, $\kappa = 0$ denotes agreement no better than chance, and negative values denote systematic disagreement. The conventional benchmarks for interpreting $\kappa$ come from @Landis_1977: values in $[0.21, 0.40]$ are "fair," $[0.41, 0.60]$ "moderate," $[0.61, 0.80]$ "substantial." Empirical studies of peer review across fields routinely land in the fair-to-moderate range, which is sobering: it means the categorical verdict on a borderline paper carries real stochastic content, and the decision an author receives is one draw from a distribution rather than a deterministic reading of merit. ### A Worked Example The code below simulates the measurement model in @eq-rating-model and reports both reliability statistics, making concrete how rater severity and noise erode agreement. We draw latent qualities for a set of manuscripts, add reviewer-specific severity and idiosyncratic noise, threshold the continuous ratings into accept/R&R/reject verdicts, and compute the ICC of the continuous scores and Cohen's $\kappa$ of the categorical verdicts for a pair of reviewers. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(42) n_papers <- 200 # manuscripts n_reviewers <- 3 # reviewers per paper sigma_q <- 1.0 # SD of true manuscript quality sigma_b <- 0.6 # SD of reviewer severity (fixed rater effect) sigma_e <- 0.8 # SD of idiosyncratic rating noise # True latent quality of each manuscript, and each reviewer's severity. q <- rnorm(n_papers, mean = 0, sd = sigma_q) b <- rnorm(n_reviewers, mean = 0, sd = sigma_b) # Ratings r_ij = q_i + b_j + e_ij (rows = papers, cols = reviewers) ratings <- sapply(seq_len(n_reviewers), function(j) { q + b[j] + rnorm(n_papers, mean = 0, sd = sigma_e) }) # --- ICC via a one-way variance decomposition (reliability of a single rater) --- grand_mean <- mean(ratings) paper_means <- rowMeans(ratings) ms_between <- n_reviewers * sum((paper_means - grand_mean)^2) / (n_papers - 1) ms_within <- sum((ratings - paper_means)^2) / (n_papers * (n_reviewers - 1)) icc <- (ms_between - ms_within) / (ms_between + (n_reviewers - 1) * ms_within) # --- Cohen's kappa on categorical verdicts for reviewers 1 and 2 --- # Threshold continuous ratings into reject / R&R / accept. to_verdict <- function(x) cut(x, breaks = c(-Inf, -0.5, 0.5, Inf), labels = c("reject", "RnR", "accept")) v1 <- to_verdict(ratings[, 1]) v2 <- to_verdict(ratings[, 2]) tab <- table(v1, v2) p_o <- sum(diag(tab)) / sum(tab) # observed agreement p_e <- sum(rowSums(tab) * colSums(tab)) / sum(tab)^2 # chance agreement kappa <- (p_o - p_e) / (1 - p_e) cat(sprintf("Single-rater ICC: %.3f\n", icc)) #> Single-rater ICC: 0.301 cat(sprintf("Observed agreement (reviewers 1 & 2): %.3f\n", p_o)) #> Observed agreement (reviewers 1 & 2): 0.415 cat(sprintf("Cohen's kappa (reviewers 1 & 2): %.3f\n", kappa)) #> Cohen's kappa (reviewers 1 & 2): 0.154 ``` ::: The simulation reproduces the empirical regularity: with realistic severity and noise, single-rater reliability is modest and categorical $\kappa$ lands in the fair-to-moderate band of @Landis_1977. Raising `sigma_b` or `sigma_e` relative to `sigma_q` drives both statistics toward zero, which is the formal statement of a familiar complaint—reviewing is noisier than authors wish—and the justification for the institutional responses that surround it: multiple reviewers to average down noise, an AE to discount severity, and the editor's argument-weighing synthesis to recover signal that any single verdict discards. ## Replication and Transparency {#sec-review-transparency} A measurement procedure is only as credible as the evidence it screens, and the top marketing journals have moved decisively toward **research transparency**: authors of empirical papers are increasingly required to deposit data and analysis code so that published results can be reproduced. From the reviewer's standpoint this adds a verification task—do the supplied materials regenerate the reported numbers?— and from the field's standpoint it raises the validity bar in @tbl-decisions by making the third criterion, validity, externally checkable rather than taken on faith. Reviewers should treat a transparency package as part of the submission and weigh its completeness alongside the manuscript's arguments. ### Data Editors and Data-and-Code Policies Verification of computational results has become a distinct stage of review, often performed by a dedicated data editor rather than by the referees. Economics moved first. The American Economic Association announced a data availability policy in 2003 and implemented it in 2004, and extended it to its new field journals between 2009 and 2012; *Econometrica* and the *Journal of Political Economy* adopted policies at about the same time [@vilhuber2020reproducibility]. Those policies required posting but did not check the materials. The AEA appointed its first Data Editor in January 2018 and adopted a revised Data and Code Availability Policy in July 2019, under which replication packages are requested before acceptance and their reproducibility is checked, through a third party when the data are restricted [@aea2019datapolicy; @vilhuber2020reproducibility]. The AEA's data-editing operation had processed more than 3,200 manuscripts by late 2026, most of them in no more than two rounds [@aeadataeditor2026summary]. Business journals followed. *Marketing Science* adopted a replication and disclosure policy in 2013 [@desai2013replication]. *Management Science* introduced a data and code disclosure policy effective June 2019 [@mgmtsci2019datapolicy], and a large reproducibility study of papers published under it, involving more than 700 reviewers and nearly 500 articles, found that more than 95 percent of articles could be fully or largely reproduced when data access and computing requirements were not obstacles; when articles with inaccessible data were included, the share fell to 68 percent. Before the policy, only 12 percent of articles provided replication materials voluntarily [@fisar2024reproducibility]. The *Journal of Marketing* adopted a research transparency policy for submissions from 2023, and in 2025 the American Marketing Association extended a common policy to all its journals, under which authors must provide replication data and materials before final acceptance; at the *Journal of Marketing Research* every conditionally accepted manuscript passes through a verification step by a data editor [@ama2025transparency]. The *Journal of Consumer Research* requires a data and materials availability statement with every submission.[^42-transparency-pages] [^42-transparency-pages]: *Journal of Marketing* Policy for Research Transparency, approved July 2022 and applied to submissions from 1 January 2023 (ama.org/journal-of-marketing-policy-for-research-transparency); *JCR* research ethics page, revised September 2026 (consumerresearcher.com/research-ethics). For the referee, the existence of a data editor changes the division of labor without removing the referee's responsibility. The data editor checks that the code reproduces the reported numbers. The referee still judges whether those numbers answer the question: whether the design identifies the effect, whether the measures capture the constructs, and whether the conclusions follow. A package that reproduces perfectly can still support an invalid inference. ## The Credibility Revolution and Research Integrity {#sec-credibility} The transparency requirements above did not arise in a vacuum. They are the operational residue of roughly a decade of self-examination, often called the **credibility revolution** or the **replication crisis**, during which psychology, economics, and the quantitative social sciences (marketing among them) reconsidered how much of their published record they actually believed. For a reviewer this history is not a curiosity. It supplies the specific checklist of failure modes a referee is now expected to screen for, and it explains why the field added the institutional machinery (preregistration, registered reports, data deposit, forensic re-analysis) that surrounds the classical review process described above. This section maps that terrain. It begins with the evidence that the literature was less reliable than assumed, turns to the unresolved statistical debates the crisis reopened, then to the forensic methods and integrity cases that data transparency made possible, and closes with a neutral tour of the marketing-specific methodological disagreements a referee will encounter and should be able to frame fairly. ### The Replication and Credibility Crisis {#sec-cred-crisis} The intellectual spark is usually credited to @simmons2011falsepositive, *False-Positive Psychology*, which showed by simulation and live demonstration that exploiting **researcher degrees of freedom**, the undisclosed choices about exclusions, conditions, covariates, and stopping rules that every analysis involves, can manufacture statistically significant support for essentially any hypothesis, driving the false-positive rate far above the nominal five percent even when no effect exists. The authors proposed disclosure remedies (the well-known "twenty-one-word solution"). @gelman2014forking sharpened the point with the metaphor of the **garden of forking paths**: a researcher need not consciously run many analyses to inflate error rates, because the single analysis actually run is contingent on the data observed, so the *p*-value is uninterpretable without a pre-specified plan. The disagreement here is not about whether the mechanism is real (it provably is) but about how much of the published literature it has actually contaminated and how aggressively the field should respond, a distinction worth preserving when a reviewer raises the concern. ::: callout-note ## Controversy: the paper that broke psychology's confidence in itself The credibility revolution has a specific trigger, and it is worth knowing, because the logic that produced it applies unchanged to marketing. The field's standard methods were used correctly, by a respected researcher, at a top journal, to demonstrate something almost nobody believed. **2011 — the paper.** @bem2011feeling publishes *Feeling the Future* in the *Journal of Personality and Social Psychology*, reporting nine experiments in which participants appear to be influenced by stimuli presented *after* their responses. The methods are conventional. The statistics are conventional. Eight of the nine studies reach significance. **2011 — the response, in the same issue.** @wagenmakers2011psi reply that the correct inference is not that precognition exists but that the field's standard analytic practice is broken: exploratory analysis presented as confirmatory, and *p*-values interpreted without regard to the prior implausibility of the hypothesis. Their argument generalizes immediately—if these methods produce this result, what are they producing everywhere else? **2012 — the replications fail.** @ritchie2012failing report three unsuccessful attempts to replicate the retroactive-recall effect. Notably, they had difficulty placing the paper: journals that had published the original were not obviously in the business of publishing failures to replicate it, which became an argument about publication incentives in its own right. **Why this is in a marketing book.** Bem's paper is the field's cleanest natural experiment on its own methods, precisely because the hypothesis was one nobody wanted to accept. When a method yields a conclusion the field is prepared to believe, the method is not tested. Every reform in this chapter—preregistration, registered reports, disclosure standards, data posting—descends from a community concluding that the conventional pipeline could manufacture support for anything. Marketing runs the same pipeline on hypotheses that are *entirely plausible*, which is a harder case to audit, not an easier one. ::: The empirical question, how replicable is the literature, was addressed by large coordinated projects. The @osc2015reproducibility replicated 100 psychology studies and found that roughly one-third to one-half met various replication criteria, with replication effect sizes about half the size of the originals. @camerer2018replicability replicated social-science experiments published in *Nature* and *Science* and successfully reproduced about thirteen of twenty-one, again with attenuated effects. The picture is worse where independent observations are expensive. In experimental asset markets the unit of analysis is the market, not the trader, so a study with 160 traders in ten-trader markets has sixteen observations. @huber2026assetmarkets ran preregistered replications of 17 results from four prominent studies in the *American Economic Review*, *Journal of Finance*, *Review of Financial Studies*, and *Review of Finance*, collecting 166 new markets with 1,544 participants; one of the originals, on self-control, had rested on eight markets per condition. Each primary test was sized for 90 percent power to detect two-thirds of the original effect. Only 3 of the 14 results originally reported as significant replicated, and in the working-paper version the average replication effect was 2.9 percent of the original [@huber2024assetmarketswp]. Induced excitement, depleted self-control, and the share of female traders all failed to predict bubbles, with point estimates of the wrong sign. Two findings survived: cognitive reflection, fluid intelligence, and theory of mind predicted trading earnings (though the latter two at roughly 60 and 40 percent of their original size), and experience roughly halved the bubble measures when the same traders traded a second market. The working paper also notes that some of the original treatment comparisons were run in separate sessions instead of being randomized within a session. A referee reading a market-level experiment should therefore check two things: how many markets per arm there are, and whether treatments were assigned within a session. A non-replication is ambiguous, however: it can mean the original was a false positive, or that the replication differed in some hidden but consequential way. The *Many Labs* projects [@klein2014manylabs1; @klein2018manylabs2] addressed this by running identical protocols across many sites, finding that most effects were robust across samples while a minority varied, evidence that contextual heterogeneity is real but does not by itself account for most non-replications. @fig-cred-timeline arranges these landmarks. The honest synthesis, which a reviewer can state as genuine convergence rather than as one camp's opinion, is that replication rates sit materially below 100 percent and effect sizes shrink on replication, while the mix of causes remains debated. Archival replication looks different, and a recent strategy case shows what it can and cannot deliver. @bettis2016replication distinguish a *narrow replication*, which reruns the original design on the original sample and is mainly confirmatory, from a *quasi-replication*, which keeps the design but changes the sample to test robustness or generalizability. @kofford2026materiality do both for @flammer2013csr, an event study of investor reactions to environmental news, and then extend it. The narrow replication recovers the original average reactions almost exactly. The quasi-replication adds a decade and finds the same time trends in decade means. The regression version of the trend test went less well. The authors could not exactly reproduce Flammer's coefficients, which they attribute to differences in how the control variables were built, and in their extended sample the trend was significant for eco-friendly events but not for eco-harmful ones [@kofford2025materialitywp]. They also attribute small differences in average returns to CRSP's corrections of historical data, so even a database the whole field shares is not fixed over time. A referee reading an archival replication should ask which tables were reproduced and which were not, and whether the data vintage is reported. @sec-mf-carbon-replication works through the case, including an arithmetic audit of its tables. ::: callout-note ## Controversy: how bad is the replication rate? A fight about the number itself The headline finding that roughly a third to a half of psychology studies replicated became one of the most cited results in social science, and it was contested directly, in *Science*, by four senior researchers. The exchange is short—both pieces occupy the same page—and unusually instructive, because it is a disagreement about statistical method conducted over a statistic about statistical method. **2015 — the estimate.** @osc2015reproducibility report the Reproducibility Project: Psychology, replicating 100 studies with the original authors' materials. **March 2016 — the challenge.** @gilbert2016comment argue the project systematically understated replicability: that many replications differed from the originals in ways likely to matter, that the sampling of studies was not representative, and that the statistical criteria used to declare a replication failed were themselves biased toward failure. Their conclusion is that the data are consistent with a much higher reproducibility rate than reported. **March 2016 — the response, same page.** @anderson2016response, writing for 44 members of the collaboration, reply that the critique's own assumptions are optimistic, that its preferred benchmark relies on a subset of studies chosen in a way that favors the conclusion, and that the original estimate stands. **How a referee should hold this.** The prudent position is not to pick a number. It is to notice what both sides concede: replication rates are below 100 percent, replication effect sizes are systematically smaller than originals, and the *causes*—false positives, hidden moderators, methodological drift between original and replication—cannot be separated from the aggregate statistics alone. That is enough to justify every reform in this chapter without needing to settle whether the true figure is 40 percent or 60. Registered reports relocate the review process itself: the referee evaluates the question and the design rather than the result, which removes the incentive to reverse-engineer a clean story from a messy dataset. Early outcome evidence is encouraging; @soderberg2021registeredreports found that registered reports scored higher on rigor and quality dimensions than comparison papers. The mature position is not that preregistration is mandatory for all work but that it disciplines **confirmatory** inference without displacing **exploratory** analysis, provided the exploratory portion is labeled honestly. The journal-level counterpart is the Transparency and Openness Promotion (TOP) framework [@nosek2015top], which the data-deposit norms in the preceding section instantiate. ### Statistical-Significance Debates {#sec-cred-significance} The crisis reopened a foundational and still-unresolved argument about statistical significance itself. The American Statistical Association took the unusual step of issuing a formal statement [@wasserstein2016asa] clarifying what a *p*-value is **not**: it is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true, and statistical significance is not practical importance. There is broad agreement on these negative claims and continued disagreement on what, if anything, should replace null-hypothesis significance testing; the ASA's own follow-up [@wasserstein2019beyond] surveyed the options and pointedly declined to endorse a single replacement. Three reform proposals now compete, and a referee should recognize them as live rather than settled. The **redefine** camp [@benjamin2018redefine] proposes lowering the default threshold for new discoveries from .05 to .005, treating the interval between as merely suggestive. The **justify** camp [@lakens2018justify] replies that no single threshold fits all contexts and that researchers should transparently justify the alpha they adopt given the costs of each kind of error. The **abandon** camp [@amrhein2019riseup; @mcshane2019abandon], the last of which is led in part by a marketing and statistics scholar, argues for retiring the dichotomous significant-versus-not verdict entirely and treating *p*-values as one continuous piece of evidence among many. @tbl-cred-alpha summarizes the three positions. The accurate summary for the book is near-universal agreement that a bright-line *p* < .05 is misused, alongside genuine disagreement on the remedy. | Position | Core proposal | Representative work | |---|---|---| | Redefine | Lower the default discovery threshold to .005; .005--.05 is "suggestive" | @benjamin2018redefine | | Justify | No universal threshold; justify alpha from error costs and study goals | @lakens2018justify | | Abandon | Retire the significant/not-significant dichotomy; treat *p* as continuous evidence | @amrhein2019riseup; @mcshane2019abandon | : Three competing responses to the misuse of statistical significance. The field has not converged on a winner. {#tbl-cred-alpha} ::: callout-note ## Controversy: the significance wars, in order @tbl-cred-alpha states the three positions; the sequence in which they arrived explains why none of them won, and a referee who knows the order will read a methods section differently. **2016 — the professional body intervenes.** The American Statistical Association issues a formal statement on *p*-values [@wasserstein2016asa]. This is unusual: scholarly societies do not normally rule on how to interpret a statistic. The statement is almost entirely negative—six principles about what a *p*-value is not—and it deliberately stops short of prescribing a replacement. **2018 — a threshold is proposed, and immediately contested.** @benjamin2018redefine, with a large multidisciplinary author list, propose lowering the default discovery threshold to .005. @lakens2018justify reply, with an author list of comparable size and overlapping fields, that no universal threshold can be right and that researchers should justify alpha from the error costs of the specific decision. Two large coalitions of methodologists, publishing near-simultaneously, reaching opposite conclusions from the same premise that .05 is misused. **2019 — a third camp says the question is wrong.** @amrhein2019riseup and @mcshane2019abandon argue for retiring the dichotomy entirely. The same year, the ASA's own follow-up [@wasserstein2019beyond] surveys the options and pointedly declines to endorse one. **How to use this at the desk.** The disagreement is real, so a referee cannot demand adherence to any one camp. What all three positions share is a rejection of the bright line applied mechanically, and that shared ground is enough to support a concrete request: report effect sizes with intervals, state the inferential threshold and why it was chosen, and do not describe a result as absent because it failed to cross .05. Those are compatible with redefine, justify, and abandon alike—which is why they are the requests worth making. ::: Running underneath this is the longer-standing **Bayesian versus frequentist** question: whether to quantify evidence with *p*-values and confidence intervals or with posterior probabilities and Bayes factors. The Bayesian side [@rouder2009bayesian; @wagenmakers2018bayesian] emphasizes that Bayes factors can quantify evidence *for* a null hypothesis and sidestep several *p*-value pathologies, while the frequentist-reform side is well represented by the ASA materials above. Modern practice increasingly treats the two as complementary and reports both; the chapters on Bayesian modeling develop the machinery a reviewer would check. ### Forensic Data Analysis and Integrity {#sec-cred-forensics} Data transparency did more than let reviewers regenerate reported numbers; it enabled a class of **forensic** methods that probe published results for arithmetic and statistical impossibilities, and it made possible the independent re-analyses associated with the blog *Data Colada*. The methods matter more than any individual case, so we lead with the toolkit, summarized in @tbl-cred-forensic-tools. | Tool | What it checks | Source | |---|---|---| | *p*-curve | Whether a set of significant findings reflects a real effect or selective reporting, from the distribution of significant *p*-values | @simonsohn2014pcurve | | Specification-curve / multiverse | Runs and displays all defensible analytic choices rather than one, exposing fragility | @steegen2016multiverse; @simonsohn2020speccurve | | GRIM | Whether a reported mean is arithmetically possible given the sample size and integer responses | @brown2017grim | | Excess-uniformity checks | Whether improbable similarity across conditions signals fabricated data | @simonsohn2013justpostit | : The forensic toolkit for screening published quantitative results. SPRITE, a related raw-data reconstruction method, circulates as a preprint and is cited here by lineage to GRIM rather than by a fabricated identifier. {#tbl-cred-forensic-tools} **P-curve** [@simonsohn2014pcurve] infers whether a body of significant findings reflects a genuine effect or selective reporting by examining the shape of the distribution of significant *p*-values. **Specification-curve** or **multiverse analysis** [@steegen2016multiverse; @simonsohn2020speccurve] formalizes running and reporting *all* reasonable analytic specifications rather than a single favored one, so a reader can see whether a result depends on a particular defensible choice. **GRIM** [@brown2017grim] performs a deceptively simple arithmetic check: given a sample size and integer-valued responses, only certain means are possible, and a reported mean that is not on that list signals an error. And @simonsohn2013justpostit showed that excessive uniformity or improbable similarity across conditions can reveal fabricated data from the statistics alone, an argument for routine data posting. These are exactly the checks a transparency package now lets a referee, or a later reader, perform. The remainder of this subsection describes a small number of prominent integrity cases. It does so in a deliberately measured, court-reporter register: every factual claim is anchored only to public records, namely retraction notices, official investigation outcomes, and dated published analyses. Where matters remain contested or are the subject of litigation, that is stated as such, and no allegation is asserted as settled fact. The pedagogical point is what the forensic methods and data transparency can reveal, not a verdict on any person. Consider first the field-experiment literature on honesty pledges. A 2012 article in *PNAS* [@shu2012signing] reported that signing an honesty declaration *before* rather than after reporting information reduced dishonesty, using auto-insurance mileage data among other studies. In 2020 a registered set of replications co-authored by several of the original authors did not reproduce the effect [@kristal2020signing]. In 2021, *Data Colada* published a post (post number 98, dated August 2021) reporting anomalies in the field-experiment data underlying the 2012 paper, and *PNAS* subsequently published a retraction of the article [@pnas2021retraction]. The accurate public-record summary is therefore: the 2012 article was retracted in 2021; a replication by several of the original authors had failed to reproduce the effect; and an independent analysis reported anomalies in the underlying field data. Public reporting has attributed the questioned data to a particular source, but because responsibility is contested and related matters have touched litigation, the book assigns no blame. A second sequence concerns several papers co-authored by one researcher. A 2015 article in *Psychological Science* [@gino2015authenticity] was retracted in 2023, a fact recorded in the journal's published retraction notice [@psychsci2023retraction]. In 2023 *Data Colada* published a four-part series ("Data Falsificada," posts 109 through 112) reporting anomalies across several co-authored papers; the relevant institution conducted an internal investigation, and several papers were retracted. Defamation litigation related to these allegations has been reported in public sources, and elements remain contested. The book states only that the matter has been the subject of litigation and that the allegations remain contested, without characterizing the merits. The durable lesson for a reviewer is structural rather than personal: arithmetic checks like GRIM, distributional checks like *p*-curve, and above all the routine posting of raw data are what make independent verification possible, which is precisely why the transparency requirements in the preceding section have teeth. ### A Marketing Case Without Fabrication {#sec-cred-marketing-case} Both sequences above turn on questioned data, and both were resolved—to the extent they were resolved—by retraction. That is the vivid failure mode, and it is not the common one. Marketing's own best-documented episode involves no allegation of fabricated data, no retraction, and no misconduct finding, and it is arguably the more instructive case for exactly that reason. The claim was that portfolios formed on customer-satisfaction scores earn abnormal stock returns [@fornell2006; @aksoy2008; @fornell2016]. Five independent teams failed to reproduce it: @jacobson2009 and @jacobson2009a located the effect in a handful of technology firms, @ittner2009 found nothing under standard multifactor asset-pricing tests, @osullivan2009 found nothing after standard risk adjustment, and @bell2014portfolio reopened how the portfolios should be formed at all. When the argument returned to the *Journal of Marketing* in 2016, the journal published the critiques in the same issue as the claim [@kumar2016satisfaction; @sorescu2016; @bharadwaj2016; @fornell2016a]. Two of those commentaries report that they could not evaluate the result at all, because the trading strategy on which it rested had not been disclosed. The strategy was productized as a publicly traded fund launched weeks after publication, so the claim has since accumulated a decade of live out-of-sample record. @sec-satisfaction-anomaly assembles the full record; @sec-satisfaction-meta supplies the meta-analytic magnitudes against which the headline should have been read. Several features of this episode are worth a reviewer's attention. Nothing in it required anyone to fabricate anything: an undisclosed estimator, a threshold chosen without justification, and a sample window that happened to contain an unusual era are sufficient on their own. The published exchange, which looks like the system working, is also what allowed the dispute to close without resolution—printing both sides substitutes the appearance of adjudication for adjudication itself. And the affirmative and null results are asymmetrically distributed across research groups, which is information a reader should weigh and a citation count will not reveal. The episode also shows where financial-interest information actually surfaced. The fund's SEC registration statement discloses that its adviser was also its index provider and that a named individual—the creator of the underlying measure and an author of the studies establishing its predictive power—held a controlling interest in both the adviser and the index organization (@sec-satisfaction-anomaly quotes the filing). Securities regulation compelled that disclosure to investors, and it is public. Whether an equivalent statement would reach a reader of the journal articles depends on a journal's disclosure policy, and marketing has historically asked less here than medicine does. The reviewer's question is the one the submission form may not pose: does any author hold a financial position that gains value if this specific result is believed, and would a reader be able to find that out? As elsewhere in this section, the book asserts no verdict on any person's conduct; the public record consists of the published papers, the published commentaries, and a fund's reported performance, and it is sufficient for the methodological point. The remedies are the ones this chapter has already argued for: disclosed estimation procedures, preregistered portfolio-formation rules, and out-of-sample tests as a condition of publication rather than an afterthought. ### How the Field Argues in Public {#sec-cred-public-argument} The satisfaction episode is unusual in scale but not in kind. Marketing conducts a surprising amount of its quality control in the open, through a genre most readers never encounter because it sits in the back pages: the published comment, the rejoinder, and the erratum. A doctoral student who has never read one should, because this is where the field's methodological standards are actually set—not in editorials about rigor, but in specific people telling specific people that a specific equation is wrong, under their own names, permanently, with a DOI. ::: callout-note ## Controversy: duelling in the back pages of *Marketing Science* Three sequences, each a matched pair or triad published by the journal itself. A reader who wants to know which party was right must still do the work themselves. ::: ::: callout-note ## Controversy: the retraction wave, 2021–2023 The credibility revolution reached marketing's own journals as retractions rather than as debate.
