The sequence matters, because the evidence that the proposal is hard to implement safely was already on the record three months before the proposal appeared in print. **2022–2026 — the load.** *Organization Science* convenes an AI task force and reports its findings as an editorial. @gartenberg2026more document a 42 percent rise in submission volume since the public release of ChatGPT in late 2022, alongside declining writing quality that they attribute primarily to AI-generated content, and the same pattern in the reviews themselves: AI-drafted referee reports show lower writing quality and less topical diversity than human-written ones. Their conclusion is a diagnosis, not a remedy—that current tools, amplified by publish-or-perish incentives, are pushing the system toward an equilibrium of more rather than better research. **2023–2025 — why it is *shadow* AI.** @wang2025policies analyse the AI policies of 439 high-impact and 363 middle-impact journals and find that 83 percent of the high-impact set have written guidance, converging on a narrow permission: transparency, human oversight, and AI restricted to auxiliary tasks such as grammar checking or reviewer finding. The binding constraint is confidentiality. A manuscript under review is not the referee's to disclose, and uploading it to a third-party model is disclosure. That is the rule the later evidence is measured against, and it is why undisclosed use has a name. **July 2025 — the exploit.** *Nikkei Asia* reports on 1 July that preprints from institutions in eight countries carry text hidden from human readers—white type, microscopic point size—instructing any language model that processes the file to return a positive review only. @lin2026hidden catalogues eighteen such manuscripts and classifies four distinct prompt designs, from a bare instruction to a full substitute evaluation rubric. The episode establishes the premise that everything after it argues about: some referees were already feeding manuscripts to models, or authors would not have bothered addressing the models directly. **November 2025 — the measurement.** Pangram Labs applies a trained detector to roughly 70,000 reviews submitted to ICLR 2026 and reports that 21 percent are fully machine-generated, with more than half showing some degree of AI involvement. The vendor reports a false-positive rate on the order of one in 10,000 and validates against 2022 reviews as a negative control. This is a commercial detection product reporting on its own accuracy, and should be read with that in mind; it is cited here as the first attempt to put a number on undisclosed use, not as a settled one. **March 2026 — the number is contested.** @saha2026enforceable make the objection that the measurement invites. Journal policies do not forbid all model use by referees; they forbid everything except polishing, paraphrasing, and grammar correction of an otherwise human-written report. Distinguishing a polished human review from a generated one is therefore the discrimination that matters, and the authors build a dataset spanning degrees of human–AI collaboration and run five detectors against it. All five flag some merely-polished reviews as machine-generated, none is accurate enough to support an accusation, and their conclusion is that public estimates of policy violation are overstated because detectors cannot separate the permitted case from the prohibited one. The book's own pattern applies: as with the replication rate in @sec-cred-crisis, the headline number was contested before the debate that quotes it had finished. **June 2026 — the audits.** Two independent teams test whether an AI reviewer can be moved without changing any scientific content. @li2026gaming rewrite only the abstract—no new results, no methodological change, no knowledge of the reviewing model—and report an attack success rate near 38 percent, with ratings rising 1.31 points for one reviewer model and 0.88 for another on a ten-point scale, and above 50 percent success when the original AI review had recommended rejection. They price the attack at about five minutes and one dollar per submission. @yang2026repackaging go further, running a closed loop that feeds the AI reviewer's own feedback back into presentation-level revisions—abstract, contribution framing, related work, discussion—while holding methods, figures, proofs, and numbers fixed. Across three mainstream AI reviewers they report a 75.1 percent success rate and a mean gain of 1.21 points out of ten, and note that repositioning related work outperforms surface polishing. Their characterization of the failure mode is the one a referee should remember: the models are easier to impress than to convince, and they confuse a limitation being addressed with a limitation being resolved. **September 2026 — the proposal.** @bhargava2026fighting publish *Fighting Fire with Fire* in *Management Science*, arguing that the answer to AI-accelerated submission volume is not to keep AI out but to bring it inside where it can be governed. Their design is deliberately narrow: a model acts as a structured front-end diagnostic on clarity, method, and internal inconsistency; it issues no accept-or-reject recommendation; its assessment is disclosed to authors for response before human referees see the paper; human referees and editors retain authority throughout; and every use is logged and auditable within journal infrastructure rather than happening privately on a referee's laptop. They model review as an information-processing system under a capacity constraint, and the argument's sharpest point is that the AI signal does not need to beat a human to help—a noisier signal still improves the system if it reallocates scarce expert attention. They also name the principal risk themselves: if every referee reads the same machine assessment, their judgments become correlated, and the system acquires a shared blind spot it did not previously have.[^42-ffwf-summary] [^42-ffwf-summary]: The modelling framing summarized here follows the account published by the UC Davis Graduate School of Management, [gsm.ucdavis.edu/blog/fighting-fire-fire-how-ai-can-help-sustain-future-peer-review](https://gsm.ucdavis.edu/blog/fighting-fire-fire-how-ai-can-help-sustain-future-peer-review), alongside the article itself. **September 2026 — three commentaries, same issue.** *Management Science* prints all three immediately behind the target article, on pages 7394 through 7398. @dai2026sound concedes the governance point—open governance beats shadow use—and rejects the premise: rising submission volume is not an existential threat, human fatigue with derivative work is a more discerning detector than any model, and a system trained on what the field has already rewarded cannot recognize the novelty the field claims to want. His test for any proposed tool is a single question, does it ask more of human judgment or less. @jiang2026shadow agrees that the real question is not whether AI enters review but whether its use stays informal and hidden or becomes transparent and accountable, then lists what the proposal does not resolve: who is answerable when the model is wrong, how authors perceive procedural fairness, and where the line now falls between objective checking and evaluative judgment. @terwiesch2026fax makes the structural objection. Improving referee throughput preserves an architecture that AI has arguably made optional, and building a faster version of the existing process is building a better fax machine rather than asking what scientific communication should look like now. **No rejoinder.** The issue closes at page 7398. The authors did not reply in print. Three observations for a reviewer. First, note what nobody in the exchange disputes. Not one of the four pieces argues that AI should be kept out of review entirely, and not one argues that it should decide anything. The consensus is narrower and more useful than the disagreement: undisclosed private use is the worst available option, and final authority stays human. Second, the audits and the proposal answer different questions, which is why both can be right. @bhargava2026fighting model the review system's throughput under load; @li2026gaming and @yang2026repackaging test an AI reviewer's robustness against an author who is optimizing against it. A front-end diagnostic that authors see and respond to is, by construction, a diagnostic that authors can optimize against, and the audits put a price on doing so. Third, this is the chapter's cleanest live instance of the pattern described in @sec-cred-public-argument: a journal printing every side and adjudicating none of them. Unlike every other episode in this chapter, you can still watch this one resolve. ::: ### Verification, Judgment, and Volume {#sec-review-ai-division} The *Management Science* exchange concerns how a journal should govern AI inside its own process. A parallel discussion among economists, conducted largely on Substack during 2026, asks a prior question: which parts of reviewing machines can now do, which parts remain human, and what happens to the system when the cost of producing a manuscript falls. The posts are not peer-reviewed and several of them argue by projection rather than evidence, but they are where much of the profession's thinking about the problem was first worked out, and they converge on a common division of labor. **What machines can verify.** The tasks that AI tools perform well are checks against something external to the reviewer's judgment: whether code reproduces the reported tables, whether a derivation is internally valid, whether cited works exist and say what they are cited for, whether numbers agree across the text, tables, and appendix, and whether claims are supported by the evidence presented. @kim2026peerreview proposes that journals use AI tools to verify mechanical reproducibility at scale and to critique validity, possibly as a pre-filter or as an additional reviewer, while an open repository accumulates verified descriptive claims. @ransom2026fixing goes further and proposes a verification organization that would certify an empirical manuscript, with code and data checked by machine, before any journal reviews it, so that the certification report substitutes for a diligent but less knowledgeable referee. Practitioners report that the tools are already useful for this purpose. @cochrane2026refine describes the comments an AI reviewing tool produced on an 80-page draft as comparable to the best he had received, and @cunningham2026agents describes delegating to an agent the work of undertaking a referee report, which he distinguishes from writing one. These accounts are consistent with the systematic evidence that model-generated feedback is often judged helpful but has limitations [@liang2024llmfeedback]. **What humans must still judge.** None of these writers proposes that machines decide. The residual human task is the one @sec-review-refereeing identifies as the hardest: judging originality, importance, and intellectual contribution. @goldsmithpinkham2026research argues that AI depreciates execution skills such as coding, data cleaning, and drafting, while knowledge of which questions matter, taste for credible research designs, and deep institutional knowledge become more valuable. @kim2026peerreview draws the implication for journals: they should concentrate human review on what machines cannot verify, including theoretical, qualitative, and methodologically complex work and research using private or proprietary data. **What happens to volume.** The concern that unites the posts is economic. AI lowers the cost of producing a competent manuscript. If submissions rise while the supply of expert referees does not, the scarce input becomes human attention. @cunningham2026research argues that research and publishing have become two different activities, with research easier and publication in valued outlets about to become much harder. @ransom2026fixing lists three disruptions: a fixed pool of referee time facing more submissions, language models that misread manuscripts, and wider variance in the quality of what is submitted. @kim2026peerreview expects that variance to run from hollow work to the frontier. The evidence through 2026 is more measured. @goldsmithpinkham2026journals reports that editors of 16 economics journals he contacted did not feel overwhelmed as of mid-2026, that submissions to the *American Economic Review* were flat, and that growth was faster at journals with low or no submission fees, while working-paper output rose by about a quarter at arXiv and the NBER between 2025 and 2026, mostly from researchers who were already publishing. @tbl-review-ai-division summarizes the resulting division of labor. First, every machine check operates under the journal's policies on confidentiality and AI use, and a referee may not run a manuscript through a tool the journal does not permit (@sec-review-refereeing). Second, machine verification is itself a measurement procedure with error, and the audits above show that AI reviewers can be moved by presentation alone. Third, if every referee relies on the same tool, referees' errors become correlated, which undermines the independence on which the aggregation of reports depends (@sec-aggregating-reviews). ### A Tour of Marketing's Methodological Debates {#sec-cred-marketing-debates} A marketing referee evaluates work across an unusually wide methodological range, and several long-running debates recur often enough that a reviewer should be able to frame each one neutrally, recognizing both the contribution and its standard critique rather than mechanically penalizing a method some camp dislikes. Each debate below is stated in two or three sentences and forwarded to the chapter where it properly lives; the home chapters develop them in full. **Structural versus reduced-form modeling.** Should a study estimate the primitives of a behavioral or economic model (structural), enabling counterfactual and welfare simulation, or prioritize clean identification of a specific causal effect through design and quasi-experiment (reduced-form)? The economics credibility revolution [@angrist2010credibility] sharpened design-based inference, while structural advocates [@chintagunta2006structural] argue structural models answer policy questions reduced-form cannot, with internal cautions on both sides about weak instruments [@rossi2014rich] and undisciplined structural assumptions [@mazzeo2006keepitreal]. The causal-inference and structural-modeling chapters develop the trade-off. **Formative versus reflective measurement.** In reflective measurement the latent construct causes its indicators; in formative measurement the indicators compose the construct, so dropping one changes its meaning, and misspecifying the direction biases structural estimates [@bollen1991conventional; @jarvis2003critical; @diamantopoulos2008formative]. A skeptical strand questions whether formative "constructs" are latent variables at all and proposes content-validity-first alternatives [@rossiter2002coarse]. This debate is developed where constructs and variables are distinguished (@sec-construct-vs-variable) and in the measurement-scales chapter. **The PLS-SEM controversy.** Partial Least Squares path modeling is popular in some marketing subfields and distrusted in others; critics argue it lacks a true latent-variable model and yields biased estimates with unreliable fit heuristics [@ronkko2013pls], while proponents reply that the critiques target outdated versions and that PLS suits prediction-oriented, formative, and small-sample work [@henseler2014pls]. This is an unusually clean critique-plus-rejoinder exchange in one journal, developed in the structural-models chapter. **Measuring advertising returns.** Can observational attribution methods recover the causal effect of advertising on sales, or are large randomized experiments effectively required? Evidence that ad effects are tiny relative to sales variance [@Lewis_2015], that brand-keyword paid search delivered near-zero incremental value in a large field experiment [@blake2015], and that observational methods diverge substantially from experimental benchmarks [@gordon2019measurement] pushes toward experiments for incrementality, while attribution modeling [@li2014attribution; @berman2018attribution] remains useful for allocation under stated assumptions. The advertising and causal-inference chapters develop the convergence. **The nudge-effectiveness debate.** How large and reliable are choice-architecture "nudge" effects in aggregate? A 2021 meta-analysis reported a moderate positive average effect [@mertens2022nudging], while reanalyses argued that the effect is not distinguishable from zero once publication bias is modeled [@maier2022nonudge] and that heterogeneity precludes expecting uniform effects [@szaszi2022noexpect]. This is as much a dispute about meta-analytic method as about nudges, and it is developed in the nudges chapter. **Mediation-analysis critiques.** Bootstrap and Baron-Kenny-style mediation from observational designs is ubiquitous in consumer research, but critics argue that without experimental manipulation of the mediator a mediation claim is causally unidentified [@bullock2010mechanism], while a constructive-reform position urges better practice (manipulated mediators, moderation-of-process, sensitivity analysis) rather than abandonment [@pieters2017mediation]. The causal-inference chapter develops the identification requirements. **The common-method-bias debate.** When predictor and outcome come from the same respondent at one time, shared method can inflate observed correlations; one position catalogs this as a serious, pervasive threat requiring design and statistical remedies [@podsakoff2003commonmethod], while another argues the blanket assumption is overstated and that some popular post-hoc corrections do more harm than good [@spector2006urbanlegend]. The surveys and measurement-scales chapters develop the practical safeguards. **Online-panel and MTurk data quality.** Crowdsourced samples democratized data collection but raised concerns about non-naivete, inattentive responding, and bots; early validations argued the data are reliable and diverse [@buhrmester2011mturk; @paolacci2014turk], later work documented worker non-naivete [@chandler2014naivete], and a recent exchange disputes whether alarming invalid-response rates reflect inherent platform failure [@webb2022toogood] or remediable design and screening choices [@keith2024anecdotal]. The surveys and data chapters develop the concrete safeguards (attention checks, geolocation and bot screening, preregistered exclusion rules). ### An Index of the Book's Documented Controversies {#sec-cred-controversy-index} Each debate above, and several episodes not on that list, is developed somewhere in this book as a **Controversy** callout: a dated, chronological account of what was published, by whom, and in what order, with every claim traceable to a cited source. @tbl-controversy-index is the index. A student who reads only the marketing column will mistake local history for the whole argument. ## Key Takeaways - External peer review is recent: editors decided alone for most of publishing history, written referee reports date from 1832 at the Royal Society, and mandatory external review became universal only after the Second World War (@tbl-review-history). - Journals bundle communication, certification, and archiving. Working papers have taken over communication; certification for hiring and tenure is what journals still uniquely supply, which is why the journal hierarchy (@tbl-review-tiers, @tbl-review-utd) carries career consequences. - A journal is an owner, a publisher, an editorial team, an office, and a referee pool. Editorial titles carry different decision rights at different journals (@tbl-review-titles). - At top economics journals, about 4 to 12 of every 100 submissions receive a revise-and-resubmit (@tbl-review-funnel), the median accepted paper takes about 21 months to acceptance and three years to print (@tbl-review-timeline), and a typical paper passes through several journals (@fig-review-lifecycle). - Over fifty years, top-five submissions doubled, acceptance rates fell from about 15 to about 6 percent, and articles became nearly three times longer (@tbl-review-trends). - Data editors now verify computational reproducibility; AI tools increasingly verify code, mathematics, citations, and consistency, while judgments of originality and importance remain human (@tbl-review-ai-division). - Reviewing is reciprocal labor that also buys proximity to the frontier and calibration about what makes a paper publishable; record it so it counts. - The editorial pipeline (@fig-review-pipeline) is a sequence of gates—plagiarism and duplicate checks, editor suitability screening, AE assignment, reviewer synthesis—and most attrition happens at desk screening and the first round. - A publishable paper must simultaneously offer **novelty**, **relevance**, and **validity**; validity failures are usually fatal because they cannot be reframed away. - A good report is short, numbered, separates **major** from **minor** comments, and closes with a **roadmap**; it supplies arguments, never a verdict count. - Refereeing (@sec-review-refereeing) is expert advice to an editor. Every comment is either a **requirement**, supported by an argument the editor can evaluate, or a labeled **suggestion** the authors may decline. A request belongs among the requirements only if some outcome of it could change the recommendation (@sec-review-pivotal). A revise-and-resubmit is a contract: state every requirement in the first round and accept the paper once they are met. - Referees miss most planted errors and are swayed by author prominence, network proximity, and agreement with their priors (@tbl-referee-evidence); structured reading and explicit criteria are the corrective. - Review is a measurement problem (@eq-rating-model): rater **severity** and noise make verdicts stochastic, single-rater reliability (@eq-icc) modest, and categorical agreement (@eq-42-kappa) typically only fair-to-moderate—which is exactly why journals use multiple reviewers and an argument-weighing editor rather than a vote. - The **credibility revolution** (@sec-credibility) supplies the modern referee's failure-mode checklist: forking paths and researcher degrees of freedom inflate false positives, replication rates sit below 100 percent (@fig-cred-timeline), the significance debate (@tbl-cred-alpha) remains unresolved, and forensic tools (@tbl-cred-forensic-tools) plus open data are what make independent verification, and the integrity record, possible.
